In the war between Senators Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen for who will be
the next Majority Leader, a psychological operation is being carried out
against all of us.

When Van Hollen announced his challenge, Schumer's response was petulant. He
didn't explain why he was the better choice. He didn't say what he'd do
differently, even though different is exactly what voters across the country
just voted for.

Instead, Schumer fell back on process. He has the votes, he insisted, so a
contested election and a public debate are unnecessary. It's like he doesn't
think he should have to apply for the job at all.  
  
The Washington media, as uninterested in the world outside Washington as
Schumer is, covered it as a backroom, Washington-centric story. Headlines
blared Schumer's claim that he already has the votes, framing the entire issue
as a _fait accompli_ requiring no further discussion. No comment about the old
guard maintaining the levers of power, no explanation of how much it's in
Schumer's interest to close off debate, no acknowledgment that it is a
Washington playbook trying to shape people's perception of what's possible.

## "I have the votes"

"I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer said last
week in response to Van Hollen's challenge.

On Saturday, _The Hill_ reported that "Schumer's allies" expect he'll win an
"overwhelming majority" of votes to become leader.

"We're done here," declared Adam Jentleson, former chief of staff to Sen. John
Fetterman (who has endorsed Schumer), in a social media post linking to _The
Hill_ 's story. "Time to move on and focus on delivering for Americans who put
their faith in Democrats to deliver real, tangible improvements in their
lives."

Apparently "delivering for Americans" doesn't include listening to them. A
majority of Americans, including Democrats, have consistently disapproved of
Schumer -- even after the midterm blowout.  
  
Even on the narrow question of who has the votes, it's not clear at all that
that's Schumer. The problem with Schumer's account is that, as of today, only
16 of the Democrats' 55 senators have publicly endorsed him. Van Hollen,
meanwhile, says Schumer is lying and that several senators Schumer claims as
supporters have actually endorsed Van Hollen. Schumer, he says, is trying to
manufacture a sense of inevitability to scare people out of supporting anyone
else. (Sound like the Biden White House stiff-arming any challenger to the
president?)

"The Schumer team's put out a lot of misinformation," Van Hollen told ABC's
This Week on Sunday. "They're essentially trying to instill fear in people who
may say that they're going to support me as a new leader."

Schumer is reaching for another Washington trick, too. He is trying to move
the vote up to two weeks from now, to head off the leadership debate.

"Let's not rush into a coronation," Van Hollen says.

## The Schumer Psy-Op

Manufactured inevitability is one of the oldest psychological tricks in the
Washington playbook. The beauty of it is that instead of having to win an
argument, they just declare it already over. And it isn't aimed only at
senators. It's aimed at the rest of us, too: the voters, activists, anyone
whose pressure might actually force changes, if only they thought it was
possible.  
  
Social scientists have a name for what happens next: "pluralistic ignorance."
In a 2022 [study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9399177) in _Nature
Communications_ , researchers found that 66 to 80 percent of Americans support
major climate policies. But Americans guessed that only 37 to 43 percent of
their fellow citizens did. Supporters outnumbered opponents roughly two to
one, yet the public believed nearly the opposite.  
  
Perception often becomes reality. People who think they're in the minority
tend to drift toward what they believe everyone else thinks, and they stop
pushing. "They fall into a trap of: I support this but I think other people
don't," the study's lead author, Gregg Sparkman,
[said](https://www.princeton.edu/news/2022/08/24/fighting-climate-change-
wildly-popular-most-americans-dont-know-other-people-feel).  
  
In Washington, declaring a race "over" before a single ballot is cast is a
tool of political control. It serves two audiences at once. Inside the
Capitol, leaked whip counts and "overwhelming majority" headlines signal to
undecided senators and incoming freshmen that opposing the incumbent is futile
and even career-limiting. Outside the Capitol, the message to voters is even
simpler: _there is nothing to see here, no debate worth having, and no reason
for you to call your senator.  
  
_ There's another benefit of the Schumer psy-op. By treating Schumer's re-
election as a foregone conclusion, party insiders can avoid answering the
substantive questions Van Hollen's challenge forces onto the table -- whether,
for example, Democrats should reject AIPAC money, whether they will block
funding for the war in Iran, and whether the new majority will confront
corporate power or slip back into the same cautious habits that left Schumer
with his abysmal approval rating in the first place.

## You're not alone

Another demonstration comes from an unlikely place: Saudi Arabia.

In a 2020 study in the American Economic Review, economists found that the
vast majority of young married Saudi men privately supported women working
outside the home. But they badly underestimated how many other men agreed,
even their own neighbors.

So the researchers told a random group of the men the real numbers. Those men
became more willing to help their wives look for jobs. Four months later,
their wives were more likely to have applied and interviewed for work outside
the home.

Nobody's mind was changed. The men just learned they weren't alone.

The most damning American example is segregation.

In a 1975 study in Public Opinion Quarterly, sociologist Hubert O'Gorman went
back to national survey data from 1968. He found that most white Americans
grossly exaggerated how many other whites still supported segregation. Their
private views had moved on. They assumed their neighbors' hadn't. So they went
along with a system most of them no longer believed in.  
  
Schumer is exploiting the same psychological blind spot. You don't have to
change anyone's mind. You only have to convince people that they're alone.

The news media failed to predict the magnitude of public discontent with the
generation in power. It doesn't seem interested in discovering the real
America now, or what people want. It prefers the binary of Democrat vs.
Republican, without ever asking: Democrat what?

Instead it covers the "race" for the majority and, of course, 2028.

Go back to sleep, America. We'll call you again in two years when we need your
vote -- er, input.
